How generation, type, and stage narrow the pool

Every Pokedle board gives you three to four major filter dimensions: which generation the Pokemon belongs to, its primary and secondary types, and whether it's a basic, stage one, or stage two evolution. Stack those correctly and you've eliminated 90% of the dex before touching anything else.

Pairing type with evolution stage immediately filters harder. A Fire/Water that's stage two evolution eliminates every legendary, every mythical, and every basic-only line from consideration.

Where players confuse similar Pokemon lines

The most common mistake on Pokedle boards involves parallel evolution lines. Players see a bipedal reptile with a specific type spread and immediately assume it's from the most obvious line—when a less famous parallel exists in the same generation with nearly identical stats and typing.

Generation-exclusive evolutions trip people up constantly. A Pokemon that evolves only in a specific game version, through a particular method, or via trading with an item gets misguessed by players who don't track regional release contexts. Check whether your candidate has any conditional evolution requirements before committing a guess.

Start each day by scanning the generation indicators before touching anything else. Ask yourself: does this board favor early-games nostalgia, mid-era complexity, or modern design language? That first impression narrows the field faster than any individual type clue.

A run of consecutive Gen 1 answers makes Gen 2 more likely tomorrow, statistically speaking. The board doesn't guarantee balance, but it tends toward variety over short windows.

Waffle answer today: how to read the solved grid

The green tiles are locked in place. Every other tile sits in a slot where it doesn't belong, waiting for a swap. When you look at the reveal card above, notice which rows and columns already contain complete words—that's your anchor point. Which swaps usually unlock two words at once

The most efficient swaps happen at intersection points where both the horizontal and vertical word share a single tile. Move that tile into its correct slot and you resolve conflicts on two axes simultaneously. These dual-impact swaps typically appear early in the solve path when you've identified two or three green anchors.

Swapping two misplaced tiles that sit in the same row or column rarely helps. You're essentially trading one wrong position for another within the same word. Look instead for tiles that are mislocated in both their row AND their column—that's where a single swap does double work.

The solver tool on this page can show you whether a particular swap affects one word or two. That's worth checking before committing if you're uncertain about the impact.

Where players leak moves they did not need to spend

The most common waste comes from swapping too early. Players see a tile they think belongs somewhere and move it immediately, only to discover later that the correct letter was already there—just buried under another misplaced tile that needed to move first.

Another leak: swapping tiles that are already in the correct position but facing the wrong direction. In Waffle, orientation doesn't matter—only location. If a tile is green, it's right. Stop touching it.

A third trap is reverting. Some players undo a swap and try a different combination without realizing they've returned to a state they'd already ruled out. Track which configurations you've tested. The archive history lets you review past puzzles and spot patterns in your own solving behavior—what worked, what didn't, and where you tend to over-swap.

How to finish tomorrow's Waffle more cleanly

Start with the longest words first. They have more fixed points, which means fewer variables to manage. Once you've placed the major words, the shorter fill-in words often resolve themselves with minimal additional swaps.

Before making any move, ask whether that swap could be avoided by moving a different pair instead. Sometimes there's a faster path that isn't obvious until you've mapped two or three moves ahead. This isn't about perfection—it's about noticing when you're about to make a redundant exchange.

Count your swaps as you go. If you're approaching the par number and haven't reached a clean board, pause and reassess. One well-chosen swap beats three experimental ones.

Does the order of swaps matter?

Yes, but not always. Swaps are commutative in the sense that the final arrangement depends on which tiles end up where, not the sequence—but some sequences get you there faster. If you're using more moves than expected, try reversing your last few swaps and testing an alternate path.

Can I solve Waffle without guessing?

Every Waffle has a deterministic solution. There are no hidden variables or probabilistic elements. If you're stuck, the issue is usually incomplete information—a tile you assumed was in the right spot actually isn't. Go back and verify your greens.

The game ends and reveals the remaining correct positions. You can still see the full solution, but you won't earn a perfect score for that day. The reveal card above shows what the completed grid looks like regardless of how you finished.

The archive shows puzzle history going back several months. Looking through past solutions, certain word lengths and grid structures recur, but the specific letters vary. Studying the archive helps you recognize structural patterns without memorizing individual answers.

Hints lock a tile in place permanently. They're useful when you're confident about a position but want to protect it from accidental swaps. If you're early in the solve and unsure, skip the hints—working through ambiguity builds the pattern recognition skills that make later puzzles easier.

The letter structure here rewards players who eliminated common vowels early. With only U as the sole vowel, narrowing down possibilities becomes straightforward once that tile turns yellow or green. The double T creates an interesting constraint—many five-letter words avoid repeating consonants, so spotting the TT pattern immediately separates this candidate from similar-looking alternatives like PATTY, PETTY, or PUTON.

Meaning and Everyday Use

Putty refers to a stiff, malleable compound used primarily in glazing and carpentry. Glaziers apply it around window panes to create a weatherproof seal. Woodworkers use it to fill screw holes, nail holes, and minor surface damage before painting. The term has also expanded into figurative usage—someone described as "putty" in another's hands suggests easy malleability or influence.

The word traces back through Dutch and Low German roots, though most modern speakers encounter it during home renovation projects rather than casual conversation. Its physical properties make it useful precisely because it stays workable long enough to shape, then hardens over time to create a durable fill.

Solving this puzzle efficiently hinges on recognizing the single-vowel constraint early. Standard opening words like ADIEU or AUDIO won't help here—they waste multiple vowels on a board where only one matters. Instead, strong opening plays for this letter distribution include words heavy on consonants: CRWTH, DRYLY, GYMPS, or RHYTH all test multiple consonants while avoiding vowels entirely.

Once the U reveals itself, the hunt narrows considerably. Words fitting the P---Y pattern with a U somewhere become the focus. Candidates like PULPY, RUNNY, or FUNKY drop away quickly if they contain vowels outside U. The double T constraint eliminates most alternatives immediately, leaving PUTTY as the primary remaining option once those tiles lock in.

Given the letter profile, conventional vowel-heavy starters lose efficiency. Words testing high-value consonants serve better here. DRYLY works well—it eliminates D, R, Y, and L from consideration while confirming nothing about vowels. CRYPT tests C, R, Y, P, and T simultaneously, which covers two of the answer's letters in a single guess.

Another effective approach uses TYPNG-style combinations to confirm the double-T placement. If both T tiles show yellow, the remaining task becomes positioning P, U, and Y correctly. Players tracking their solver history might note that double-consonant words appear roughly every twelve puzzles on average, making them predictable enough to prepare for without special strategy.

Tracking end-letter distributions separately from start-letter data often catches these clustering effects before they cause wasted guesses.

Protecting a streak requires discipline beyond raw solving ability. Never attempt the daily puzzle while distracted—split attention leads to simple transposition errors that cost the solve. Some players maintain a physical notebook alongside their digital play, recording each answer by hand. The extra cognitive step reinforces memory and provides a backup reference if app sync fails.

worgle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The answer card on this page shows a five-letter Welsh word that relies heavily on digraphs—letter pairs that function as single sounds. If you've been plugging away using English intuition, you probably noticed certain tiles behaving strangely. That's not a bug. That's Welsh doing what Welsh does.

Worgle answer today: what the Welsh letter pattern is hinting at

Welsh spelling isn't decorative noise. Every digraph represents a distinct phoneme that appears far more often than its English equivalent would suggest. On today's board, the answer contains either DD, LL, or TH—three of the most reliable signal letters in Welsh. A careful player usually notices these clusters light up early if they prioritize vowels and common Welsh consonants over standard English high-frequency letters. Check the answer above against your current position. If you're sitting on two correct letters but haven't placed the digraph yet, you're probably looking at a word where one of those pairs holds the second or fourth position.

The reveal card confirms whether your guess landed on the right sound structure. Archive links on this page let you pull yesterday's solution and compare patterns across recent days—a habit that builds faster than grinding blind.

How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

Most players encounter three main digraphs in Welsh puzzles: DD (voiced dental fricative, like "this" but softer), LL (lateral fricative, no English equivalent), and NG (always starts a syllable in Welsh, never ends one). These aren't rare edge cases—they show up in roughly one out of every three or four valid answers.

Don't try to map them to English sounds during play. Instead, treat each digraph as a single unit. When you see a green tile on the second position, that's telling you the entire pair belongs there, not just one letter. Overthinking the pronunciation will slow you down more than it helps.

The solver tool on this site handles digraph validation automatically, so if you're second-guessing whether a guess is accepted, run it through there before wasting a turn.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

English Wordle players lean hard on letters like S, R, N, T, L. Those letters exist in Welsh too, but their frequency ranking differs significantly. W appears roughly twice as often in Welsh vocabulary compared to English. Y functions as a vowel in many contexts, appearing in final positions where English would use E or I. Starting words heavy with English-pattern letters will miss these distributions.

The other trap is assuming Q, X, and Z are dead letters. They aren't common, but Welsh has borrowed some words that use them. J appears in loanwords. The board doesn't cheat—it plays by Welsh orthography rules, which means occasionally you'll see a K where English wouldn't expect one.

If you've been stuck for two turns without placing any new tiles, switch to a word that tests a digraph position specifically. That narrow focus catches more edges than cycling through unrelated English guesses.

How to handle tomorrow's Worgle more smoothly

Build a shortlist of solid Welsh starting words before you need them. Words containing DD, LL, NG, or WR give you immediate digraph coverage. Avoid words with multiple uncommon English letters clustered together—save those slots for later rounds when you've narrowed possibilities.

Check the archive for patterns over the past week. You'll notice Welsh puzzles tend toward certain structural preferences—many answers follow a consonant-vowel-consonant-digraph-vowel pattern. Knowing that shape lets you filter guesses faster.

The hint widget gives you one confirmed letter position without costing a guess. Use it strategically rather than waiting until you're completely stuck. Early hints preserve your remaining guesses for actual solving work.

Why does Welsh use double letters differently than English?

In Welsh, double letters like DD and LL represent unique sounds, not emphasis markers. English doubles are mostly historical accidents or pronunciation guides. Welsh doubles carry phonetic meaning—if you see DD in the answer, that's one sound occupying two tiles on the board.

Can players use a normal English Wordle strategy for Worgle?

Partially. The core loop—eliminate letters, confirm positions—still works. But your starting word selection and letter frequency assumptions need adjustment. Treat Worgle as a parallel puzzle running on slightly different rules rather than trying to force English habits onto Welsh data.

The game rejects invalid guesses. Welsh has a smaller valid word list than English Wordle, so some familiar patterns won't appear as options. Stick to the accepted word database shown in the validator, or use the solver link to check questionable guesses before committing.

No. The game strips accents from input and treats accented letters as their base equivalents. You can ignore circumflexes, acute accents, and grave accents entirely—they're formatting conventions in written Welsh, not functional distinctions for the puzzle.

worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The silhouette on today's Worldle gives you a rough outline before any numbers appear. Most players spend too long staring at the shape alone. The compass heading and distance percentage do the heavy lifting once you know how to read them together.

Worldle answer today: what the silhouette should suggest first

A country's shape tells you its continent before anything else. Narrowing the hemisphere removes dozens of candidates instantly. Once you know whether you're looking at something in Africa, South America, or Southeast Asia, the remaining possibilities drop into a manageable range. The archive link on this page lets you cross-reference past shapes if you're unsure whether you've seen this outline before.

Look at the coastline curvature next. Jagged edges often point toward peninsulas or archipelagos. Smoother outlines lean toward large inland nations or continental masses. This isn't about memorizing every border—it's about recognizing visual families.

How direction and distance clues narrow the shape

The arrow shows which direction your guess sits from the target country. The percentage tells you roughly how far away you are. These two numbers work as coordinates on an invisible grid. A guess northwest of the answer at 15% distance means you're looking for something roughly 1,500 kilometers away in that relative position.

Players who treat each clue independently miss the pattern. The direction constrains which side of the equator and which longitudinal band you're hunting in. The distance then tells you whether you're in the right neighborhood or still thousands of miles off. Combining both cuts your search space dramatically after just two guesses.

If you're stuck, the solver tool on this page can reverse-engineer which countries match a given direction-distance pair. That's faster than scrolling through regional lists manually.

Why neighboring countries become the easy wrong answer

After your first guess, the game shows you exactly how far the target sits from that country. Players often assume the answer must be adjacent to their first pick. It rarely is. Distance percentages above 10% almost always rule out immediate neighbors.

The trap is familiarity. You recognize Belgium or Paraguay on sight, so you keep picking nearby alternatives that share borders with your opening guess. But the game rewards geographic thinking across continents, not micro-local knowledge. Try a country on a different landmass that shares your guess's approximate direction and distance. You'd be surprised how often the answer lands somewhere you'd never considered.

How to finish tomorrow's Worldle with fewer detours

Build a mental checklist before you guess. Continent first, then approximate size relative to known countries. Check whether the compass direction aligns with your guess's position on the map. Finally, test distance plausibility—would this country realistically sit that far from your last attempt?

The reveal card shows your solve path at the end. Reviewing that sequence helps you spot where you over-corrected or ignored a strong signal. Players who track their accuracy over time using the archive tend to improve faster than those who play reactively each day.

Questions players keep asking

Does the distance percentage represent actual kilometers or a scaled metric?

It's a proportional distance based on the shortest path between capital cities. A 5% reading means your guess's capital sits roughly 5% of Earth's circumference away from the target's capital. The math keeps things consistent regardless of where countries fall geographically.

Can players use the compass direction to pinpoint the exact hemisphere?

The arrow points toward the target from your guess's center. If your guess is east of the answer, the arrow points west. Read it backward from your current position. Combined with latitude awareness, this tells you whether the target sits north or south of your current guess.

Why did my correct answer still show multiple countries at the same distance?

Tied distances happen when countries share similar capital positions relative to your guess. Small nations clustered in regions like Central America or the Balkans often produce ties. The game breaks ties alphabetically, so your placement might differ slightly from another player's even with identical guesses.

The archive lets you replay previous days' puzzles. Each archived puzzle uses the same format and reveals the full solution history. Practicing on older boards trains your eye for silhouette patterns and hones your directional logic without affecting your daily streak.

Bookmark the solver for days when the silhouette resists easy identification. It won't rob you of the challenge—it'll help you understand which geographic assumptions were leading you astray.
